I've got the same thoughts, but went into the series with these already. If you didn't, maybe it wasn't as lopsided in perspective as I took it.

What irked me during the fall of Saigon was the image of the helicopter going off the side of the ship while a military person commented about how disgusted he felt seeing that. My understanding, from vets I met in the 80's, was the helicopters were tossed overboard when they didn't have enough fuel for a return trip and room was needed for more refugees - they rescued everyone possible from approaching smallcraft. I felt the series didn't emphasize how difficult is was for US troops & sailors to leave the people behind.

And the interesting thing about a documentary like this one is that it has the benefit of hindsight in portraying how inevitable it was that the south would fall. Again, based on vets I met in college in the 80's, they really thought they were winning/gaining ground in the late 60's - maybe the troops on the ground were fed bs to keep them going or maybe the media at home was getting tired of the war & echoing the dismissive demoralizing 'when will it end mantra of the protesters. I don't know - I was just a kid, but I remember the hippy youth(older siblings & cousins and later teachers in jr. high) thinking they succeeded in ending the war & me thinking they were full of beans.
